# Chapter 5 — Book Scaffold: `new_book.py`

*Thirty seconds of typing makes the structural commitment that the rest of the book will either keep or betray.*

**Capability — one line:** Students run `new_book.py` to scaffold their book directory and understand what each generated file does and who reads it.

**Learning objectives**

- (Apply) Run `new_book.py` against your TIKTOC.md and produce a populated book directory.
- (Apply) Populate `metadata.yaml` with title, subtitle, author, and publisher so pandoc can build a real EPUB later.
- (Analyze) Inspect the scaffold and identify which files Cowork reads at runtime versus which files only the human ever touches.

---

## Opening — the command, then the output, then the silence

You open a terminal. You are in the directory where your TIKTOC.md lives. You type one command:

```bash
python new_book.py --tiktoc TIKTOC.md --slug ai-for-designers
```

Thirty seconds later, the terminal has stopped scrolling. Forty lines of green checkmarks. The last line says `done`. You list the directory. There is a folder named `ai-for-designers/` that did not exist a minute ago. Inside it, files you did not write — `vision.md`, `architecture.md`, `chapters-spec.md`, `risks.md`, `outline.md`, `book.md`, `metadata.yaml`, `build.sh`, `README.md` — and folders: `chapters/`, `pantry/`, `images/`, `d3/`, `output/`, `styles/`.

That is the chapter's failure mode and its success at once.

The failure: a designer with ten years of client work just had a folder generated by a Python script. The instinct is to back away. The instinct is wrong, but the instinct is real. Most authors who quit here quit because they cannot read the directory — they see strangeness and assume complication. The chapter teaches you to read the directory in the next five minutes so that strangeness collapses into recognition.

The success: in thirty seconds, your TIKTOC.md has been *executed*. The chapter list you produced in the Tic TOC session is now a folder of empty chapter files waiting to be drafted. The capability statements are now stub files inside `chapters-spec.md`. Your book exists as a directory. It is the first time the TIKTOC.md becomes something other than a Word document.

This chapter teaches you what each of those files is, who reads it, and why the scaffold is the first proof that the TIKTOC.md session was the actual work.

---

## Sidebar — Installing Python in five minutes

If `python new_book.py` printed `command not found`, this is what you do. Read it, do it, move on. The rest of the chapter assumes Python 3.10 or newer is installed.

**Mac.** Three commands. Open Terminal (in `/Applications/Utilities/`).

```bash
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
brew install python
python3 --version
```

The last line should print `Python 3.12.x` or similar. If it does, you are done. If `brew` is unknown after step one, restart your terminal — Homebrew sometimes needs PATH refresh.

**Windows.** Three commands. Open PowerShell as Administrator (right-click → Run as Administrator).

```powershell
winget install --id Python.Python.3.12 -e
python --version
py -m pip --version
```

The second line should print `Python 3.12.x`. The third confirms pip (Python's package installer) is alive. If `winget` is missing, install App Installer from the Microsoft Store first.

**Linux (Ubuntu/Debian).** Three commands. Open Terminal.

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip
python3 --version
pip3 --version
```

Both versions should print without error.

That is the install. No virtual environments, no `pyenv`, no version managers. Five minutes. Move on. Philip Guo's 2014 documentation of Python's rise as the teaching language at top U.S. universities included one persistent finding: install friction was the single largest predictor of disengagement in the first week. The sidebar exists to refuse that pattern. You are not learning Python in this book. You are running one script that someone else wrote so a directory appears.

---

## The command and its arguments

```bash
python new_book.py --tiktoc TIKTOC.md --slug ai-for-designers
```

Two arguments. That is the entire interface.

`--tiktoc` points to the TIKTOC.md file you produced in Chapter 4. The script reads it. It looks for the chapter list (the section your Tic TOC session output as Part 8), the metadata block (title, author, audience), the three-act arc, and the capability statements. These become the scaffold's structural commitments. If the TIKTOC.md is missing a chapter title or a capability statement, the scaffold reveals it — empty files, blank specs, named gaps. This is a feature. The first time the TIKTOC.md is held to a deterministic standard is the first time its vagueness is visible.

`--slug` is the directory name. It becomes the project folder, the EPUB filename, the URL slug if you ever put the book online, and the KDP working title. Kebab-case, lowercase, no spaces. `ai-for-designers`, not `AI for Designers`. The slug is the only argument you cannot easily change later — every other field in the scaffold is editable; the slug is baked into paths.

That is it. No interactive prompts, no global config file, no choices to make. This is by design. Audrey Roy Greenfeld's Cookiecutter [Greenfeld & Greenfeld, *Two Scoops of Django*, multiple editions; Cookiecutter project documentation, 2013–present] established the canonical Python scaffolding interface: one command, sensible defaults, no global state. `new_book.py` is in that direct lineage. If you find yourself wanting more flags, you are usually about to make a decision you should make in TIKTOC.md instead.

**Idempotency.** If you run the command twice in the same directory, the script refuses to overwrite. This matters. Running it a second time after edits will not destroy your work. If you genuinely want to rebuild from scratch, delete the directory first. [verify — confirm current `new_book.py` idempotency behavior against the script in `SCRIPTS/`]

## What Cowork reads at runtime

The scaffold makes a structural distinction the rest of the book depends on: *some files are read by Cowork; some files are read by you*. The distinction is not enforced by extension or folder. It is enforced by the chapters that follow. Knowing which is which collapses most of the cognitive load of using this pipeline.

**Cowork-facing files** (Cowork reads these when generating drafts):

- **`TIKTOC.md`** — the spec. The Chapter Writer prompt reads this first. The voice section, chapter list, capability statements, and bridge questions are all consumed at runtime. If a single file in your directory is the contract, this is it.
- **`book.md`** — the book-level summary. Cowork uses this for cross-chapter coherence (knowing what's coming in Chapter 9 while drafting Chapter 5). It is generated from TIKTOC.md but may be edited.
- **`pantry/`** — one notes file per chapter, plus shared `_lib_` files. Cowork reads the pantry file for the chapter it is currently drafting. This is Chapter 6's subject. For now, know only that Cowork looks here for the research it cannot do itself.
- **`chapters/`** — Cowork writes here. It also reads existing files here (to avoid overwriting what is finished and to maintain inter-chapter continuity).
- **`metadata.yaml`** — pandoc reads this at build time. Cowork glances at it for title and author when generating front matter.

That is the Cowork interface. Five things. Nothing else in the directory is read by the automation. This is deliberate. If Cowork could read every file you wrote, every stray note would condition the draft, and you would spend the rest of the project second-guessing what to leave lying around.

This file-level separation is older than AI tooling — it is the literate-programming distinction Knuth named in 1984: "instead of imagining that our main task is to instruct a computer what to do, let us concentrate rather on explaining to human beings what we want a computer to do" [Knuth, 1984, *Literate Programming*, The Computer Journal 27(2), 97–111]. The directory splits the explaining (human files) from the instructing (machine files) at the filesystem level.

---

## What the human uses

The rest of the directory exists for you. These files were generated, but they are not read by the automation. They are the working notebook the pipeline does not see.

- **`vision.md`** — the one-paragraph statement of what the book is and who it is for. Generated from the TIKTOC.md vision section. Read it when you have lost the plot. Update it when the book's purpose actually changes (rarely).
- **`architecture.md`** — the three-act arc, the prerequisite map, the load-bearing chapters. Generated from TIKTOC.md Parts 5 and 6. Read it when you are deciding whether a chapter belongs in this book at all.
- **`chapters-spec.md`** — the full chapter list with capability statements, learning outcomes, and bridge questions. This is your editor's reference. When you reach Chapter 8 and start rewriting Cowork drafts, this is the file you check the draft against.
- **`risks.md`** — the contested claims, the aging risk register, the open questions from TIKTOC.md Part 11. Read it before you publish.
- **`outline.md`** — the human-readable table of contents. This is the file you copy into Substack newsletters or emails to colleagues when explaining what you are writing.

There is one rule about these files: *do not let Cowork edit them*. The temptation, when Cowork produces a strong chapter draft, is to ask it to update `architecture.md` to reflect the new direction. Resist. These are the files where the author thinks. Letting the automation rewrite them is letting the automation think about what the book is. That is the fluency trap one floor up.

## The build script — `build.sh` and `output/`

The last piece of the scaffold is a shell script. You will not run it until Chapter 11. But it is generated now so the contract is visible from the start.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Concatenates chapters/*.md, runs pandoc, writes EPUB + PDF to output/
cat chapters/*.md > _working/combined.md
pandoc _working/combined.md \
  --metadata-file=metadata.yaml \
  --epub-cover-image=cover.jpg \
  -o output/${SLUG}.epub
pandoc _working/combined.md \
  --metadata-file=metadata.yaml \
  --pdf-engine=xelatex \
  -o output/${SLUG}.pdf
```

This is the entire build. Read it twice. Three things are doing all the work:

1. **Concatenation** — every file in `chapters/` is glued together in filename order. This is why chapter files are numbered `01-`, `02-`, `03-`. The number is not decoration; it is the build order.
2. **Pandoc** — the universal document converter [MacFarlane, John, *Pandoc User's Guide*, 2006–present, pandoc.org]. It takes Markdown plus a metadata file and produces EPUB and PDF. The `metadata.yaml` schema is not invented by AI+1; it is pandoc's own. Title, author, language, rights, description — all standard pandoc fields.
3. **Output** — everything lands in `output/`, which is gitignored. The output directory is not the book; it is the *artifact of building the book*. The book is in `chapters/`. Treat `output/` as disposable. If you delete it, the next `./build.sh` recreates it.

The Turing Way [The Turing Way Community, 2022, *The Turing Way: A handbook for reproducible, ethical and collaborative research*, Zenodo] calls a build script "the covenant that anyone can reproduce the artifact." `build.sh` is your covenant with future-you. Six months from now, when you want to rebuild after a typo fix, you run one command. No memory required.

Quarto [Posit, *Quarto*, 2022–present, quarto.org] and Jupyter Book [Executable Books Community, 2019–present] offer more elaborate build systems for scientific publishing. They are excellent. They are also overkill for a $1 Kindle textbook produced by one author. `new_book.py` ships pandoc + bash because that combination has been stable for fifteen years and will be stable for another ten.

## Worked example — the `ai-for-designers` scaffold

This is the directory `new_book.py --tiktoc TIKTOC.md --slug ai-for-designers` produced. Every file present, every file named, every reader identified.

```
ai-for-designers/
├── TIKTOC.md                  [Cowork] the spec; read first by Chapter Writer
├── book.md                    [Cowork] cross-chapter coherence summary
├── vision.md                  [Human]  one-paragraph book purpose statement
├── architecture.md            [Human]  three-act arc + prerequisite map
├── chapters-spec.md           [Human]  full chapter list + capability statements
├── risks.md                   [Human]  contested claims + aging risk register
├── outline.md                 [Human]  human-readable TOC, for sharing
├── README.md                  [Human]  three-line description, what to run
├── metadata.yaml              [Build]  pandoc reads this at build time
├── build.sh                   [Build]  the EPUB + PDF build script
├── chapters/                  [Cowork writes here, build script reads here]
│   ├── 00-frontmatter.md
│   ├── 01-the-fluency-trap.md
│   ├── 02-the-ai-plus-one-designer.md
│   ├── ... (one .md per chapter)
│   └── 99-back-matter.md
├── pantry/                    [Cowork reads here; Chapter 6 populates]
│   ├── _lib_glossary.md       (shared, prefixed _lib_)
│   └── (one chapter-research-XX.md per chapter, generated in Ch 6)
├── images/                    [Build]  PNG figures (Chapter 9 fills)
├── d3/                        [Build]  interactive D3 HTML (Chapter 9 fills)
├── styles/                    [Build]  pandoc CSS + LaTeX templates
├── output/                    [Build]  EPUB + PDF land here, gitignored
└── _working/                  [Build]  pandoc temp files, gitignored
```

Three audiences. The directory makes the audiences visible. This is the figure to commit to memory — Cowork-facing files in one mental color, human-facing files in another, build-facing files in a third.

**The fully populated `metadata.yaml` for `ai-for-designers`:**

```yaml
---
title: "AI for Designers"
subtitle: "A Practitioner's Guide to AI+1 for Graphic Design"
author: "Your Name"
publisher: "Your Studio Press"
rights: "© 2026 Your Name. All rights reserved."
language: en-US
date: 2026-05-28
description: >
  A short practitioner handbook for working graphic designers
  building one client-facing or workshop-ready AI+1 textbook.
identifier: ai-for-designers-v1
cover-image: cover.jpg
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---
```

Eleven fields. Every one of them lands in the EPUB metadata pandoc generates. Designers respect populated artifacts — Wilson and the Software Carpentry tradition argues that "people read directories before they read code" [Wilson, Greg et al., 2014, "Best Practices for Scientific Computing," PLoS Biology 12(1)]. The same is true of a metadata file. Show the values. Don't leave `<your-title-here>` placeholders for the reader to wonder about.

## AI Wayback Machine — Kristen Nygaard

Wikipedia: "Kristen Nygaard."

Nygaard (1926–2002) was a Norwegian computer scientist who, with Ole-Johan Dahl, invented object-oriented programming by building Simula in the 1960s. His central conviction was that programs are models of the world, and that the *structure* of the program — the objects and their relationships — must mirror the structure of what is being modeled.

The scaffold you just ran is Nygaard's idea applied to a book. Your TIKTOC.md describes a book. `new_book.py` produces a directory that mirrors that description. Chapters are folders of files. The audience structure (Cowork files vs. human files vs. build files) mirrors the production structure. If the model is wrong, the directory is wrong, and the wrongness shows up at every later step. Nygaard's later career — leading the "No to EU" campaign in Norway through the 1990s — is one of the reasons he is worth knowing about; his computer science was inseparable from his commitments to who got to model what.

**Try it:** Ask Claude: "What did Kristen Nygaard mean when he said programming is modeling? How does that idea show up in a directory layout for a book?"

## Exercises

**Exercise 5.1 (Apply).** Run `python new_book.py --tiktoc TIKTOC.md --slug <your-slug>` for your own book. Confirm the directory was created. List its contents. Verify that the top-level files include `TIKTOC.md`, `book.md`, `vision.md`, `architecture.md`, `chapters-spec.md`, `risks.md`, `outline.md`, `metadata.yaml`, and `build.sh`. Verify the `chapters/`, `pantry/`, `images/`, `d3/`, `styles/`, and `output/` folders exist. If anything is missing, re-read the Python install sidebar and try again.

**Exercise 5.2 (Apply).** Open `metadata.yaml`. Populate every field — title, subtitle, author, publisher, rights, language, date, description, identifier, cover-image. Save. The values you put here will appear in the EPUB Kindle generates in Chapter 11. Use real values, not placeholders.

**Exercise 5.3 (Analyze).** Open `TIKTOC.md` inside your new directory. Confirm the chapter list from your Tic TOC session is present. Now answer in one sentence: which file does Cowork read first when generating a chapter draft? (Hint: it is named in the previous section.) If you cannot find the answer in your own scaffold, you have either skipped Chapter 4 or your TIKTOC.md is missing a chapter list — return to `/c1` in Tic TOC before continuing.

## Still puzzling

- **What if the same shared note belongs in two books — is `_lib_` a copy, a symlink, or a reference?** The current scaffold copies. Symlinks would be cleaner but break on Windows file shares. [verify — confirm current `_lib_` handling]
- **Does `new_book.py` ever need to be rerun against the same directory?** The script refuses to overwrite. If your TIKTOC.md gains a chapter after the scaffold exists, you currently add the chapter file by hand and update `chapters-spec.md`. A `--sync` flag is being discussed but not yet shipped.
- **Why isn't there a `make` or `Justfile` alternative to `build.sh`?** Solo authors do not need a task runner; bash is universal. If you teach in a Linux/Mac shop and prefer `make`, the build is one target — easy to port.
- **Is `chapters-spec.md` redundant with `TIKTOC.md`?** Not quite. `chapters-spec.md` is the *editable* view of the chapter contract; `TIKTOC.md` is the *source* view. In practice you may edit one and forget to update the other. The author's discipline is to treat `TIKTOC.md` as canonical and regenerate the spec on changes.

---

## What would change my mind

If the scaffold ever produced a directory the author had to spend more than fifteen minutes understanding, the argument that "the directory is itself instructional" would collapse. The whole bet is that a designer can read the scaffold in five minutes and feel oriented. If first-time readers consistently report otherwise, the scaffold is too clever or too verbose, and the right answer is to flatten it further — fewer files, fewer folders, more inline comments. The directory is a teaching artifact before it is a build artifact. If it stops teaching, it has stopped working, regardless of how cleanly pandoc consumes it.

---

## Bridge to Chapter 6

The directory exists. `TIKTOC.md` is in place. `chapters/` is full of empty stubs waiting to be drafted. But Cowork cannot draft yet. It does not know what sources to cite, which domain examples land, which contested claims to flag. It has the spec but not the research.

The pantry is empty.

Chapter 6 runs the Chapter Research Gatherer — the automation that produces one notes file per chapter — and then teaches you to read those notes critically. The pantry is what stands between a Cowork draft worth rewriting and a Cowork dump.
